title: Top Gaming pick: Roblox - BofA
content:
Top Gaming pick: Roblox - BofA 
Roblox is evolving into a hit factory capable of delivering a consistent cadence of large-
scale viral experiences. While investors are concerned that 2026 year over year growth
slow materially against the extraordinary comparable set by Grow a Garden in 2025 (now the largest video game launch by concurrency in history) we believe those concerns would dissipate as 2026 unfolds. The evidence points to Grow a Garden not as a random lightning strike but as the first major proof point of investments made across 2024 and early 2025 in discovery, creator economics, infrastructure, and AI. By the time investors look to CY27 and beyond, we expect the narrative to shift toward renewed cost leverage and durable growth, supporting upside to valuation and our Buy rating.
Why now: the ’26 Y/Y comps debate is mispriced
Roblox’s Q3 2025 results underscore a platform whose flywheel—users, content velocity, monetization—is accelerating, not peaking. DAUs reached 151.5M (+70% Y/Y) and Hours 39.6B (+91% Y/Y), while bookings surged 70% Y/Y to $1.92B—with strength beyond a single title (engagement for experiences outside the top 10 rose 58% Y/Y; spending outside the top 10 rose 40% Y/Y). These datapoints show broad based health, even as Grow a Garden sets records, and imply that tough 2H26 comps are being offset by more titles scaling faster and better monetization tools. Management has already flagged that 2026 reported growth may be pressured by comps and new safety policies, but also emphasized the tailwinds from new tech hitting the platform in late Q1/early Q2 2026 and the long-term margin story beyond 2026.
Importantly, Roblox raised FY25 bookings guidance and highlighted that bookings growth has outpaced the company’s ability to deploy growth investments—a near term headwind to margins, but a bullish leading indicator for future output (content) and monetization. This framing supports buying ahead of 2026 while the market anchors on comps rather than on cadence.

title: Why Honduras Matters More Than It Looks in the Nic...
content:
Why Honduras Matters More Than It Looks in the Nicaragua Play
I still think the December 2, 2025 pardon of former Honduran president Juan Orlando Hernández matters most in the Nicaragua phase of what increasingly looks like a Donroe Doctrine sequencing. The logic isn’t ideological; it’s operational. Honduras borders Nicaragua, and in Central America, proximity is leverage.
What complicates and sharpens that leverage is what happened immediately after the pardon. Just days after Hernández was released from U.S. prison, Honduras’ Attorney General, Johel Antonio Zelaya, issued a domestic arrest warrant on December 9, 2025. These charges are separate from the U.S. drug case and center on fraud, money laundering, and the alleged diversion of more than $12 million in state funds tied to the Pandora corruption scandal. As of today, the warrant remains active, and Hernández is reportedly staying out of the country as a result. That timing matters. It preserves the pardon’s geopolitical signaling to Washington while keeping Hernández legally sidelined at home, an outcome that quietly stabilizes the transition without forcing an immediate reckoning.
The pardon itself helped reset Honduras political alignment at a sensitive moment. Nasry “Tito” Asfura’s November 30, 2025 election win, certified just before year end returned a pro U.S. government after a leftist interlude. That puts Honduras back in position as the frontline state for pressure on Daniel Ortega’s Nicaragua. Intelligence cooperation, border enforcement, migration control, and indirect support for opposition networks all become easier with a cooperative government next door. This fits the broader sequencing with Venezuela first, Nicaragua next, Cuba as the eventual capstone, with Mexico running in parallel.
It’s also important to be precise about who controls what right now. Asfura isn’t yet in office and Honduran inaugurations don’t happen until January 27 so the current left leaning Castro administration still controls the justice system and issued the warrant. Asfura has no formal authority to intervene at this stage, and he’s made no public move to revoke or enforce it. That ambiguity is useful. It allows the incoming government to distance itself from Hernández’s baggage while benefiting from the political realignment his pardon helped unlock. If the warrant quietly stands after inauguration, it can be framed as respect for judicial independence or anti corruption credibility, rather than political retaliation though any such interpretation remains speculative.
There’s a colder, transactional message running through all of this. The pardon signals to regional elites that alignment still buys protection at the strategic level, even if legal accountability doesn’t disappear entirely. In Nicaragua’s case, that signal can be more powerful than sanctions alone. It encourages hesitation, defections, and recalculation inside Ortega’s circle without requiring overt U.S. escalation. As WOLA has noted, this reflects a broader shift in U.S. policy with a willingness to tolerate imperfections in friendly regimes to secure hemispheric control and block rival influence.
Taken together, the sequence turns Honduras into a disciplined pressure point rather than a liability. Hernández is neutralized without destabilizing the transition, Asfura inherits a cooperative relationship with Washington, and Nicaragua faces a tighter perimeter just as pressure ramps up through tools like early 2026 tariffs. There’s always a risk of backlash, but structurally, this looks less like inconsistency and more like careful board positioning, locking pieces in place before the next move.

title: Trump's announcement to ban institutional investor...
content:
Trump's announcement to ban institutional investors from buying single family homes is addressing a real problem that mainstream housing debates often ignore or downplay.
Large companies like Invitation Homes, American Homes 4 Rent, and Blackstone are systematically buying single family homes in specific neighborhoods particularly majority Black communities that were devastated by the 2008 foreclosure crisis when families lost everything. 
Once these companies own enough homes in a neighborhood, they control the market.
In some suburban areas around Atlanta and Phoenix, they own up to 78 percent of all rental homes. 
This matters because when these corporate landlords buy homes, the character of entire neighborhoods changes from owner occupied to renter occupied, which fundamentally shifts where wealth goes.​
Think about it this way, when you own a home, you build equity.
Your mortgage payments build your net worth, and eventually you own an asset worth hundreds of thousands of dollars. 
That's how working class families historically built generational wealth. 
But when a corporation owns the home, your rent payments go to shareholders in New York or California, not into your own equity. 
Institutional investors deliberately targeted neighborhoods with economic growth potential, the exact places working families could have climbed the wealth ladder and converted them into rental markets. 
A young family might pay $1,400 per month renting from Invitation Homes or $2,100 per month to own the same home. 
Over 30 years, one path builds wealth, the other enriches a corporation.
The eviction behavior shows how aggressive these companies can be. 
Research found that large corporate landlords in Atlanta filed eviction notices 8 percent more often than small landlords, even after accounting for neighborhood conditions. 
Some private equity firms filed evictions on literally one third of their properties every single year.
 In Atlanta in 2015, 22 percent of all rental households got eviction notices, mostly concentrated in historically Black neighborhoods. 
When you're evicted, you lose your job stability, your kids school stability, your health gets worse and your neighborhood destabilizes.
Institutional investors, under pressure to maximize returns for distant investors, adopted aggressive eviction strategies that destabilized entire communities.​
The targeting was strategic and intentional. 
These companies identified neighborhoods that had recovered from foreclosures (meaning stable), strong population growth (meaning economic opportunity) and weak price to rent ratios (meaning profit potential for them). 
They found working class communities with real economic potential and systematically converted them from owner occupied to rental controlled. 
They didn't build these neighborhoods or pioneer economic growth there, they identified vulnerable communities and extracted wealth from them.​
People who defend institutional investors claim they expand rental supply and operate efficiently, lowering rents. 
That's technically true in some ways, but it completely misses the point. 
Yes, they expanded rentals, but at the cost of homeownership access. 
When institutional investors buy single family homes, the entry level properties where first time buyers typically start and convert them to rentals, they're cutting off the traditional path to wealth building for middle income families earning $25,000–$50,000 annually. 
Those families lose the option to own, instead they're locked into renting to these corporations forever.​
Some argue that banning institutional investors won't solve America's housing shortage, we're short 2 to 4 million housing units due to zoning restrictions that prevent new construction. 
That's true but that's a completely separate problem. 
Just because we need to build more housing doesn't mean we should allow large corporations to monopolize neighborhoods and destabilize communiti[...]

content:
if you’re afraid of speaking up bc you think someone will take you out of context, or judge you, or that you'll say something which could be perceived as weird... 
the best counter is VOLUME + CONSISTENCY
meaning speak from the heart, raw, and do it often...whether it be good or bad. 
volume + consistency flattens out these tails. 
some will be good, some will be bad, it will eventually just paint a picture of a real, well-rounded personality
don't fake who you are. to be bad is better than being fake, because everyone with some sense knows they have some bad in them
without even throwing it out there to test, a tweet that starts with like "I feel like a rotten piece of shit because of xyz thing I did today"... that will probably resonate, bc people feel like that at least once each day lol. guilt or shame over something they said or did.

VOLUME + CONSISTENCY.
the world has a 24-hour memory. what you put up tmw forces what you put up today into the background.
eventually, you will have a body of work, or at least a clear voice, where people can recognize you distinctly as who you are, whatever that may be. 
and this, above everything else, is what helps defray the three things at the start of the post: criticism, judgment, and the fear of saying something odd. 
have faith that "the crowd" will see you for who you really are, whether they vocally defend you or not. 
if the criticism is dogshit, they'll see it. 
if you're being wrongly judged, they'll see it. 
if you say something odd, your "body of work" renders it less odd by comparison
that's the path out of fear, strangely, a lot of the time....overadjusting, going VIOLENTLY in the total opposite direction.

title: Why Protecting Homebuyers Might Mean Protecting Pr...
content:
Why Protecting Homebuyers Might Mean Protecting Prices
Stripped of the politics, Trump’s message is that housing is for people, not portfolios.
He’s arguing that affordability has broken down so badly that the government needs to step in and stop large institutional investors from buying more single family homes. Not force sales. Not unwind the past. Just draw a line under future purchases. The framing is moral as much as economic because families should be competing with families, not with capital pools that can bid endlessly and wait forever.
That’s why more matters. This isn’t a mass liquidation threat. It’s a demand side choke point aimed at the marginal buyer going forward.
What That Would Actually Do To Housing
At a national level, it wouldn’t magically fix prices. Big institutions don’t own most homes. But that’s not how markets move.
Prices move at the margin. by who shows up to bid on the next house. And in certain metros, especially in parts of the Sun Belt, institutional money does show up consistently. Taking that buyer out of the room cools bidding pressure in specific neighborhoods, especially at the starter home level. That’s where first time buyers feel it.
But here’s the catch: if you block institutional buyers without increasing supply, you don’t solve the system, you just rearrange it. Some homes shift back to owner occupiers. Some renters get squeezed. Some markets stall. You reduce competition in one place and increase stress in another.
This is why policies like this rarely deliver clean outcomes on their own.
Why This Starts To Look Like A Backdoor Bailout
The bailout concern isn’t crazy, and it’s not conspiratorial. It’s historical.
After the last housing crash, the government explicitly invited large investors in to stabilize prices. Foreclosed homes were sold in bulk. Rental programs were encouraged. The goal was to stop prices from falling further. It worked but it also created today’s institutional footprint.
Fast forward to now. If institutions are already under pressure with higher rates, refinancing risk, slower rent growth and then you cap their ability to keep buying, you set up a problem…how do they exit without crashing prices?
That’s where bailouts sneak in quietly.
Not as a check with the word bailout on it, but as…
• government purchase programs,
• subsidized affordability initiatives that set price floors,
• guarantees, tax credits, or financing structures that let portfolios be absorbed without market pain.
It gets sold as helping buyers. But it also protects existing holders from a disorderly unwind.
The Bigger Picture
This isn’t really about punishing Wall Street or saving homeowners. It’s about managing downside risk in a system that can’t tolerate falling home prices.
Blocking future institutional demand is politically clean. Letting prices fall sharply is not. So the tension is obvious that if you stop new buyers but still can’t allow a collapse, the state ends up backstopping the exit…directly or indirectly.
That’s how affordability policy can quietly turn into a bailout.
Not because it was the plan from the start, but because once housing becomes financial infrastructure, the government doesn’t let it fail cleanly.

content:
the most rewarding reaction on twitter, by far...
"I needed that."
it's a 2x
1. you wrote that shit hard and tight
everyone's feed is a waterfall, a firehose, or more accurately, a flushing toilet
fluff in a message halts all forward progress as the reader is either confused or exercising unnecessary brainpower to unscramble your intent
one thing that all writers/texters/emailers forget to do, before clicking send, is ask: what will the reader's first impression be upon opening this email?
not even the words. is it just a giant block of text, where the ask is buried somewhere in there without foresight or logic?
they're going to open it and their mind will say "fuck, I have to work to untangle this."
this is actually just the writer being inconsiderate and thoughtless. it's understandable. we sit there and spend so long making sure everything we wanted to say is in there, but we put no thought into:
"is this going to be easy for them to read? will they be able to tell, immediately, what response is expected?"
an email that begins or ends with "YES/NO/MAYBE" options, makes their life infinitely easier. Or a simple closed ended question. 
A considerate writer will lay their message out in a way where the reader can open it, recognize within 5 seconds "the answer is yes," reply "yes," and click send.
Boom. Zero cognitive load. Compare that to having all your delusional rambling diarrhea where it takes 3 minutes just to figure out what the f you want, plus how to answer (bc you didnt specify YES NO MAYBE).
That same principle...avoiding undue burden on the reader's mind...I think is naturally developed from reading books. Reading books makes you a better writer, because you know what a considerate writer looks like, and what an inconsiderate one.
A great quote I read said that the reader is being asked to decipher hundreds of thousands of little black squiggly lines and turn them into language. 
That's taxing on the brain. 
Don't make their job any harder than it has to be!
I suspect that "write hard and tight" isn't about perfect prose as much as it is a straightforwart, start-to-finish train of cohesive thought. 
That should be good enough to yield an emotional reaction
--
2. you correctly expressed a nuance of human nature in a way that avoided cliche, while being differentiated, insightful, and unique to this specific reader.
What you REALLY did, is you found words for loose thoughts/feelings/emotions that were floating around in the reader's head.
That's why they didn't know they needed it. They didn't have words available for it, and a thought without words is probably hidden in the subconscious waiting to emerge in defined form.
When the message arrived, the words clarified the subconscious impulse and forced it higher into your general consciousness.
Great writers always find beautiful and unique paths to express even the most mundane or overlooked details in daily human interaction, facial expression or conversation.

Scott Fitzgerald's "The Beautiful and Damned," it's always classic fiction, strangely, that leaves you with a philosophical or psychological lesson.

title: Gold Is Repricing Trust
content:
Gold Is Repricing Trust
On the surface, this looks like a simple crossover where gold’s share of global reserves are nudging past U.S. Treasuries for the first time since the 1990s.
But the real message that counterparty risk is back and central banks are reacting to it.
Reserves aren’t about return. They’re about survival. They exist so a country can stay liquid in a crisis and remain independent in a world that isn’t always cooperative. For decades, U.S. Treasuries fit that role perfectly: deep markets, stable institutions, and a dollar system that was boring in the best possible way.
What’s changed isn’t that Treasuries suddenly became bad. It’s that they became conditional. When payments, clearing, reserves, and access can be used as leverage, risk free stops meaning what it used to. Add chronic deficits and political volatility, and Treasuries start to look less like neutral ballast and more like an exposure you consciously size.
That’s the phase change. It’s slow for a long time… then obvious all at once. Gold doesn’t need to be productive. It just needs to be nobody else’s promise.
Where This Is Heading
I don’t think the dollar just disappears and we wake up in a clean gold standard reboot. The dollar still has massive network power in trade invoicing, debt markets, collateral habits, institutions. Those don’t vanish because gold gains share in reserves.
What’s more likely is quieter and messier. The world becomes more multipolar in settlement. More trade runs through regional currencies, swap lines, and bilateral deals. And gold increasingly sits in the middle as the neutral reference point when trust between blocs is thin.
That’s why central bank buying matters. This isn’t hot money chasing momentum. It’s policy. Once a reserve manager decides they want more physical gold, that demand is sticky and largely price insensitive. Since supply doesn’t respond quickly, price has to do the rationing. That’s how you get long, grinding moves higher that don’t always line up with daily risk on and risk off narratives.
At this point, gold isn’t just an inflation hedge. It’s a trust hedge with protection against the rules changing after you’ve already committed capital.
The U.S. Angle, Beyond The Headlines
Could the U.S. revalue gold to help with the debt problem? Mechanically, yes. Magically, no.
On paper, U.S. gold is still carried at about $42 an ounce, giving it a book value around $11B, even though its market value is closer to a trillion. That gap exists because the price is fixed by law and tied into Treasury Fed accounting. You can’t unlock more value without changing the statute.
There is precedent. In the 1930s, the government raised the official gold price, effectively devaluing the dollar and expanding monetary capacity. A modern version would look similar where Congress changes the statutory price, Treasury marks up its gold holdings, and the Fed credits Treasury accordingly. That balance could then be used to retire debt, fund deficits, or recapitalize parts of the system.
But this isn’t paying off the debt in any clean sense. It’s a balance sheet swap…trading interest bearing debt for base money. The cost shows up as a weaker dollar versus gold and, unless paired with real productivity gains, higher inflation. Marking gold to market alone doesn’t erase the debt; truly eliminating it would require a much higher official gold price, which is really a deliberate reset of the unit of account.
The Bigger Picture
In my opinion we’re moving into a hybrid system. Not a pure gold standard, and not the clean, dollar centric world of the post 1990s either. More fragmentation. More friendly settlement networks. More emphasis on neutral collateral.
In that world, gold’s endgame isn’t a single price target. It’s a role. It becomes the thing you settle in when you don’t fully trust the other side’s ledger.

title: The Monthly Payment That Broke the Housing Market
content:
The Monthly Payment That Broke the Housing Market
What you’re looking at here is three very different realities living in the same market. The green line is what it costs today to buy a home with current prices and rates. The blue line is what it costs to rent. The orange line is what existing homeowners are actually paying because they locked in low fixed rates years ago.
For most of the 2010s, those lines moved together. Buying wasn’t much more expensive than renting, and sometimes it was cheaper. That made moving, upgrading, or becoming a first time buyer feel reasonable.
Then Rates Reset In 2022 And Everything Broke
The cost to buy didn’t creep higher. It jumped. Monthly payments went from something like the mid $1,000s to the high $2,000s almost overnight. Rents kept rising too, but slowly and steadily. Existing homeowners barely felt it at all.
That gap is the freeze. Buyers pull back. Sellers don’t move. Inventory stays tight. Prices don’t clear the way they normally would.
Buying vs Renting Then vs Now
The relationship matters more than the absolute numbers.
Back in 2013, buying cost meaningfully less per month than renting. Through most of 2018–2021, buying and renting were roughly in line. The decision came down to lifestyle and confidence, not survival math.
Today, buying costs roughly 40% more per month than renting. That’s not a small premium. That’s a psychological wall. People feel it immediately, even if they can technically qualify on paper.
When buying is that much more expensive than renting, demand doesn’t disappear, it just waits.
What Has To Change For Affordability To Come Back
There are only a few ways out of this, and none of them are painless.
Rates can fall. Prices can fall. Incomes can rise faster than housing costs. In reality, affordability usually improves through a mix of all three and often through some economic discomfort along the way.
Here’s the hard truth…without stress in the labor market, housing doesn’t really reset.
If people feel secure in their jobs, they don’t sell. If they don’t sell, supply stays tight. If supply stays tight, prices don’t move enough to fix affordability, even if rates dip a bit.
That’s the paradox. Rate cuts driven by a strong economy tend to revive demand and push prices back up. Rate cuts driven by a weakening economy cool demand and bring supply to market. Only the second path actually improves affordability.
And psychology matters just as much as math. When people sense economic risk, they don’t rush to buy a house. They wait. That waiting itself freezes the market further, dragging out the adjustment.
So the most likely path isn’t a clean crash or a smooth recovery. It’s a long period of low transactions, awkward pricing, and frustration until either rates come down a lot, incomes catch up over time, or unemployment rises enough to force a reset.
Until that green line moves meaningfully closer to the blue one, the housing market stays stuck, not because people don’t want homes, but because the monthly payment doesn’t make sense anymore.

title: Japan’s 10 Year Just Crossed A Line
content:
Japan’s 10 Year Just Crossed A Line
A 10 year yield around 2.1% doesn’t sound dramatic if you’re used to U.S. or Australian bonds. In Japan, it’s a regime shift.
For nearly three decades, Japan’s bond market lived off the assumption that rates stay low forever. After the bubble burst, everything reinforced that belief…weak growth, falling prices, aging demographics, and a central bank willing to suppress yields at almost any cost. That’s why betting against JGBs became known as the “widowmaker trade.” People tried to call the turn for years and got crushed.
So when the 10 year moves back toward levels last seen in the late 1990s, the signal isn’t that Japan is finally normal but rather that one of the anchors holding global rates down is starting to lift.
Japan has long been a major exporter of capital because money was so cheap at home. Ultra low yields pushed Japanese institutions and global funds borrowing yen outward in search of return. As domestic yields rise, that outward flow weakens, and global funding dynamics begin to shift.
Japan’s Delayed Inflation Experiment 
What makes this moment more interesting is why yields are rising.
Japan is running a version of the inflation experiment the U.S. ran after Covid, just later, and through a different channel. After Covid, Japan slid back toward deflation as weak demand, demographics, and a less supportive global growth model reasserted themselves.
Instead of mailing checks, Japan applied political pressure to force broad corporate wage hikes. Different mechanism, same goal of getting money into the real economy and break the deflation mindset.
Wages matter because they’re what make inflation stick. You can subsidize prices or stimulate temporarily, but without rising incomes, inflation fades. Japan is trying to pry open a wage channel it couldn’t sustain for decades.
The uncomfortable reality is that if that wage and demand push isn’t continually reinforced, inflation doesn’t just cool, it collapses, drifting back toward the deeper deflation Japan knows too well. In that sense, today’s inflation isn’t the core problem. It’s the cover, a thin layer of price pressure sitting on top of a much larger deflationary structure shaped by debt, demographics, and slower global growth.
That’s why Japan is walking such a narrow line…normalize too fast and deflation returns; stimulate too little and the wage experiment fails.
Why This Matters For The Yen Carry Trade
The yen carry trade works only when funding is cheap, the yen is stable or weakening, and volatility stays low. Break any of those, and the trade starts to wobble.
A Global Downturn Usually Breaks All Three At Once
In risk off moments, leverage comes down fast. Investors sell carry assets and buy back the funding currency. Short yen positions get covered, and the yen can jump sharply. This isn’t theory because it has happened repeatedly.
Volatility is the silent killer. Carry looks great when FX volatility is low. When volatility spikes, that steady pickup turns into forced exits at the worst time. The trade is effectively short volatility.
Rate differentials can also compress quickly. In a downturn, the Fed and others usually cut. If Japan is tightening or even just not easing, the gap narrows. Suddenly the yen isn’t free funding anymore.
My View
If the world rolls into a real downturn while Japan is still normalizing, the yen carry trade becomes a global deleveraging amplifier. It doesn’t cause the downturn, but it can make it sharper by forcing unwinds across FX, rates, and risk assets.
For years, Japan was the world’s cheapest, most reliable funding source.
If that era is ending, markets don’t just reprice Japan, they reprice the assumptions built on Japan staying pinned to zero forever.

title: MSCI Let MicroStrategy Stay With Strings Attached
content:
MSCI Let MicroStrategy Stay With Strings Attached
At a basic level, MSCI chose the least disruptive path.
There was a real risk that MicroStrategy could fall out of certain indexes simply because its balance sheet no longer looks like a traditional operating company. If that had happened, it wouldn’t have been about opinions on Bitcoin, it would’ve been mechanical. Index funds would have been forced to sell. That kind of forced selling can hit fast and hard, regardless of fundamentals.
MSCI avoided that. They’re keeping MicroStrategy in their indexes as long as it continues to meet standard criteria like size, liquidity, and free float. That decision alone removes a big overhang, which explains the immediate relief rally and why people read this as bullish.
The Part Most People Are Missing
MSCI didn’t give MicroStrategy a free pass. They also tightened the rules around how much its index weight can move as the stock price swings.
In plain English…you can stay in the club, but you don’t get to swing the furniture around.
By limiting how certain inputs are adjusted, things like share count changes and inclusion factors, MSCI is reducing how much automatic buying or selling happens just because Bitcoin is volatile. That caps the upside from passive inflows during big rallies, but it also dampens downside pressure during drawdowns.
This isn’t anti Bitcoin. It’s MSCI doing what index providers are paid to do which is keep benchmarks stable, predictable, and usable for large pools of passive capital.
Why This Matters Beyond MicroStrategy
This is really about a new category of company taking shape…asset treasury vehicles. MicroStrategy just happens to be the most visible example.
Index providers were never built for companies whose balance sheets dominate the business itself. But that model is becoming more common, not just in crypto. MSCI’s decision is an early attempt to draw a line that says we’ll include you, but we won’t let balance sheet volatility distort the index.
That matters because index inclusion is a form of institutional legitimacy. Once MSCI sets a workable framework, other providers like FTSE Russell, S&P are going to feel pressure to clarify their own rules. You can already see the direction…inclusion, but with guardrails.
My View
Short term, this is clearly positive. It removes the risk of sudden index exclusion and forced selling, which is the worst kind of downside.
Longer term, it’s more nuanced. The same rules that stabilize the downside also limit how much reflexive upside MicroStrategy can get from passive flows during big Bitcoin moves. The stock still trades on Bitcoin exposure but the index system isn’t going to amplify that exposure unchecked.
Zooming out, this is what integration actually looks like. Crypto exposure isn’t being rejected by the system. It’s being absorbed slowly, cautiously, and on the system’s terms.

title: "THERE IS NO ROOM FOR MODERATION"
content:
"THERE IS NO ROOM FOR MODERATION"
moderation is a form of self-deceit. think about all the times you’ve heard someone say “everything in moderation.”
in my experience, it is ALWAYS in defense of some bad habit and comes paired with self-deceit. this is written not to offend anyone, but written sharply, and in a way that hopefully challenges your priors + forces you to think differently (isn't that what we're all here for?).
(2/5)
moderation always arrives with drinking too much, drug use, being lazy, eating poorly, doing things you know you shouldn’t be doing…deceit in both the behavior ("a few drinks never killed anyone") and in the magnitude of the behavior ("a few" as 2, when reality = 12)
underneath all addictive behavior, whether drugs, sugar, excuses, gambling, or social media, you will find the same thing: lies. 
if this is too uncomfortable to apply to yourself, apply it to others and you’ll see it hold true... deceit about the behavior/magnitude + excuses made to others, and all typically performed the guise of moderation.
taken to extremes, one could argue that moderation is synonymous with broken discipline, or a weak mind with no self-control. this is not to ruffle feathers, it is just to make you think. because moderation, in its simplest form, can be viewed as an inability to keep the promises you make to yourself.
(3/5)
lets view thru another lens...
study greatness at all levels, and tell me how much moderation you see. 
I see none. 
I consistently see a maniacal focus on perfection, people who are over-the-top obsessive-compulsive on every single detail, who view process discipline as binary, absolute and objective...psychotic yes, but in plain language they are just people who never, EVER break their own rules.
there is no room for subjective thinking, and to allow room for moderation, they would say, is just to allow room for mediocrity.
(4/5)
the final extension of this idea is in changing one’s habits and lifestyle.
from my own lived experience, as far as removing bad habits, adding new ones or making wholesale lifestyle changes… the best results come from making every single change, cold turkey, at the exact same time. overnight, the switch gets flipped, you rip out all the fucking wires at once, and then hurl all vestiges of your old lifestyle into Savonarola’s bonfire.
this is best done VIOLENTLY and with SEVERE SELF-DISCIPLINE.
the more swiftly you can discard your old habits, and the more abrupt this change is, the more likely everything is to stick.
compare...you can discard everything completely, or you can devote daily headspace to your old lifestyle/habits/"identity".
for me, nothing good has ever come from that, because "WHAT YOU FOCUS ON EXPANDS." perhaps my mind is just weak. but conceptually, devoting time and energy to old habits creates pressure, impulses repressed, that will eventually burst like a dam.
things like counting days, celebrating milestones, never worked for me, bc external validation never works...all motivation has to be internal or it won't stick... "all change comes from within."
(5/5)
in practice:
--old identity: [discarded]
--new identity: “I’m just not someone who [insert bad habit]...drinks, does drugs, etc...I used to in a prior life, but don't anymore."
can substitute anything in there...anything re: trading markets, process, philosophy, you can set it on fire and start fresh.
they are things you once did. they were the habits of an old version of you, in some bygone era. 
the memories exist, the impact of words and deeds will always exist, but when it comes to old ways of operating...as time passes, it erodes any trace of discarded prior notions and of worldviews rendered obsolete.
the days are long, they say, but the years are short...because all long terms are really just a series of short terms, and all short terms are a series of individual days. each day can be broken into micro-decisions where the "switch" has flipped from impul[...]
